app.title: Orrery — four models of the solar system
app.subtitle: Ptolemy · Copernicus · Kepler · Newton
mode.label: Model
engine.label: Construction
engine.help.ptolemaic-reframe: Accurate positions expressed with Earth at the centre. What Ptolemy was approximating.
engine.help.ptolemaic-epicyclic: Ptolemy's actual construction with Almagest parameters, errors included.
engine.help.circular: Every orbit a plain circle about the Sun, traversed uniformly. This is not Copernicus's model but the simplification it is often mistaken for — useful for seeing what the eccentric was buying him, and how much of an orbit's shape the eccentricity alone accounts for.
engine.help.nbody: Numerical integration of Newton's law of gravity. Orbits are not prescribed; they emerge — and what emerges is Kepler's ellipses, now as a consequence rather than an assumption. The integration is a modern technique: Newton himself solved the two-body case in closed form and handled the rest by perturbation.

harness.label: Overlays
harness.sightlineBend: The sight-line bends at the body because the compressed scale distorts angles measured from anywhere but the centre of the map. The line is drawn through the body rather than straight past it — a line that misses what it points at would be worse. At true scale the bend all but disappears; in Ptolemy's view, where Earth is also the centre, it vanishes.
harness.trailsEmpty: Orbits are drawn from positions actually visited, not computed in advance. Run the clock and the trail builds.
harness.trailsRecorded: {{days}} days recorded, {{step}}-day steps. Longer history is kept more coarsely.
view.scaleHint: Compressed scale shows every orbit at once; true scale keeps the distance ratios honest.
view.zodiac.label: Zodiac
view.constructionHint: Select a body to see its machinery — circles for Ptolemy and Copernicus, an ellipse for Kepler, force vectors for Newton.
view.constructionLegend: The thin circle is the deferent, the heavier one the epicycle. The open ring marks the deferent's centre; the diamond marks the equant, the point about which the epicycle's centre moves uniformly. The dashed line is the apsidal axis.
view.constructionScaleWarning: At compressed scale the curves appear distorted. Switch to true scale to see them in their true shape.

locale.label: Language
info.forceScaleNote: Vector lengths are ordered but not proportional — the Sun is over 98% of the pull, so true proportions would leave the others invisible. Exact figures are in the table.
view.forcesLegend: The blue vector is velocity, the black one the net force. The thin vectors are each body's gravitational pull, coloured by which body pulls. Lengths are ordered, not proportional — exact figures are listed under the selected body.
view.sphere.frameHint: The celestial sphere is concentric with the map, as on a traditional orrery. Sight-lines bend at the body when the observer is not the centre.
view.sphere.observerHint: The celestial sphere surrounds the observation point, which is where the sky actually belongs. The sphere is no longer concentric with the map, and the map shrinks to make room. Sight-lines still run observer → body → sphere, so they pass through the body whatever the projection does.
theme.label: Look
view.zoomHint: The mouse wheel and the + / - keys zoom the map, dragging moves it, both about the stationary point. Double-click returns to the fitted view. On the realistic scale the zoom reaches far enough to separate the Moon from the Earth; bodies that fall off the map are then shown as pointers on its edge.
engine.help.ptolemaic-almagest: The same construction driven by Ptolemy's own mean motions and his precession — what a second-century astronomer would actually have computed. His rates are excellent, but the error is paid once per revolution: over nineteen centuries the outer planets drift about a degree, Venus and Mercury by tens.
events.comparison.referenceNote: Reference from the VSOP87 theory, times in UT. Within minutes of published values — under ten for both the 2020 Mars opposition and the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn.
engine.help.vsop87: VSOP87, the analytical theory used here as the reference. Elliptical orbits with their mutual perturbations; the yardstick the three historical models are measured against.
engine.help.keplerian: Kepler's ellipses: the Sun at one focus, and a radius vector that sweeps equal areas in equal times. The same heliocentric arrangement Copernicus proposed, with the circles replaced — which is where the accuracy actually came from.
view.ellipseLegend: The curve is the orbit itself — an ellipse, not a circle. Both open rings are foci: the Sun sits on one and nothing at all on the other. The small ring between them is the geometric centre, which now governs nothing. The bright arm is the radius vector; run the clock and watch it sweep faster near the Sun.
view.osculatingLegend: The Moon is not placed by an ellipse — no fixed one fits it — so this is the two-body orbit its present position and speed imply, Earth at the focus. Run the clock and watch it breathe: the Sun's pull on the pair swings the eccentricity by a factor of three within months. That wandering is what Ptolemy chased with a crank and Newton finally explained.
calc.title: How the models were used
calc.intro: None of these models was a picture. Each was a procedure for turning a date into a number, and the numbers were the product — the Almagest is a book of tables, and Kepler spent thirty years on the Rudolphine Tables.
calc.demonstrations.intro: The handful of moments when the models disagreed about something the sky could settle. Each sets the date, the model and the vantage.
calc.working.intro: Finding {{body}} on {{date}}, as each model required it to be done. Oldest first.
calc.working.moral: The labour climbs steeply from Ptolemy to Kepler and then stops. Ptolemy needs two table look-ups and two additions; Kepler needs a transcendental equation solved by iteration, per body and per date, by hand. Newton needs no new arithmetic at all — his two-body solution is Kepler's ellipse. What changed with him is that the ellipse stopped being fitted to observation and became a consequence of a force.
calc.selectBody: Select a body on the map to see each model's working for it.
calc.ptolemy.epicycleCentre: Mean longitude of the epicycle's centre
calc.cost.ptolemy: Two table look-ups and two additions. This is what an ephemeris cost for fourteen centuries.
calc.cost.ptolemySun: One table look-up and one addition — the Sun needed no equant.
calc.cost.copernicus: Two table look-ups and an addition — much what Ptolemy's method cost, which is the awkward part of 1543: the new system was no cheaper to use and no more accurate, and its case had to rest on other grounds.
calc.cost.kepler: Newton–Raphson passes: {{iterations}} — because M = E − e sin E cannot be rearranged for E. Once per body, per date, by hand.
calc.cost.newton: No new arithmetic for one planet: the two-body problem solves in closed form to Kepler's own ellipse, so the column to the left is Newton's working too. What he added was the reason it holds — and a period that follows from the masses, which run backwards is how the Sun was weighed. Beyond two bodies there is no closed form; Newton attacked that by perturbation, and the {{evaluations}} force evaluations behind the last line are a modern stand-in he never had.
demo.venus-phases-1610.note: Kepler says three-quarters lit; Ptolemy says a crescent. With the spheres nested, Ptolemy cannot show more than half — so this is not a discrepancy but a contradiction, and it ended the geocentric system.
demo.mercury-transit-1631.note: Kepler predicted this transit in the Rudolphine Tables and did not live to see it; Gassendi watched it in Paris. Either it happens or it does not — the sharpest test a model can face.
demo.great-conjunction-1603.note: Jupiter and Saturn close at a few hundredths of a degree a day, so a small error in angle becomes an enormous one in time. The models fall days apart here.
demo.mars-opposition-1602: The Mars that broke the circle
demo.mars-opposition-1602.note: Mars is the most eccentric of the classical superior planets, so it is where circles fail worst. Kepler's eight arcminutes of leftover error came from oppositions like this one.
demo.great-conjunction-2020.note: The same crushing test, with a published time to check against: the reference lands within eight minutes of it.

bodies.label: Bodies
welcome.title: Four ways of predicting a planet
welcome.lede: The same sky, computed by Ptolemy, Copernicus, Kepler and Newton. Where they disagree is the interesting part.
welcome.point.models: Switch model in the top-left panel. Nothing else moves, so any change you see is the model's doing.
welcome.point.centre: Hold any body still — Earth for Ptolemy, the Sun for the rest — and watch every orbit redraw around it.
welcome.point.demos: Calculation & demonstrations opens the moments that settled the argument, and shows what each model cost to work by hand.
welcome.keys: Space plays and pauses, ← and → step a day, + and − zoom, Esc closes a panel. The ⓘ button in the top-right turns the explanatory text on and off.
calc.tables.ptolemy: The Almagest (c. AD 150) gives the tables and their derivation together; the Handy Tables were the working edition. Mean motions rested on Babylonian eclipse records centuries older, because only a long baseline pins a rate down — so the whole scheme leaned on somebody else's observations. Each planet's eccentricity and epicycle had to be wrung geometrically out of a handful of chosen observations. And the equation of argument changes with the epicycle's distance, so it needs two tables and an interpolation between them. The Alfonsine Tables carried all this into Latin Europe and were still in use three centuries later, re-rooted as they drifted.
calc.tables.copernicus: De revolutionibus (1543) carried tables of its own, but the ones people used were Reinhold's Prutenic Tables of 1551 — years of recomputation on Copernican parameters. They spread widely and were barely more accurate: the circles set the floor, and no amount of care in the arithmetic could lift it. Copernicus had also rejected the equant on principle and put small extra circles in its place, so what replaced Ptolemy's machinery was no simpler to tabulate.
calc.tables.kepler: The Rudolphine Tables, 1627 — twenty-six years after Tycho's observations came to him, through a war, a lawsuit with Tycho's heirs over those observations, and his mother's trial for witchcraft. Every single entry needed Kepler's equation solved by iteration, which is why he seized on Napier's logarithms partway through and bound a table of them into the result: the tables were only finishable because a new way of multiplying arrived while he worked. Vindicated by the Mercury transit of 1631, which the older constructions place on 4 November — when nobody would have been watching.
calc.tables.newton: The Principia (1687) contains no ephemeris at all. It is a book of theory, and the gap between the law and a usable table took another century of perturbation work to close. Clairaut's lunar theory first gave the Moon's apsidal motion at half the observed rate, and he came close to proposing an amendment to gravitation itself before carrying the approximation further fixed it. Mayer's lunar tables of the 1750s won a share of the Longitude Prize; tables in Newton's spirit came later still, from Laplace, Le Verrier and Newcomb.
engine.help.copernican: The heliocentric model as De revolutionibus actually describes it: each orbit an eccentric circle, with a small epicyclet replacing Ptolemy's equant. Copernicus split the eccentricity between the two, and the result follows an ellipse closely — his circles were never concentric.
info.ptolemyParts: Ptolemy gives no absolute distances. The Almagest states every measurement in parts of that body’s own deferent, which he always takes as 60 — and directions seen from the Earth are unchanged if a deferent, its eccentricity and its epicycle are scaled together, so nothing he could observe would have fixed the scale. Each body’s 60 is therefore a different real length, and these figures cannot be compared between bodies.

track.title: Where {{body}} appears, night after night
track.none: Select a body to plot the track it traces against the stars.
track.hint: Longitude runs up the plot and time across it, so this is the record an observer keeps: a body’s place among the stars on a series of nights. Where the curve doubles back the body is retrograde, and the rings mark the two stations either side of it. Ptolemy’s epicycle and Copernicus’s moving Earth were both built to reproduce exactly this shape.
